lesson.title: Turn On, Tune In, Drop Out: America's Cultural Rebellion
lesson.summary: During the 1960s, a generation of mostly young, baby boom era Americans rejected mainstream values around consumerism, sexuality, and authority, building a counterculture centered on music, communal living, and experimentation that overlapped closely with the anti-war movement.
lesson.body:
The counterculture drew its numbers and much of its energy from the baby boom, the enormous surge in births following World War II that meant an unusually large share of the American population was reaching young adulthood together during the 1960s. That shared generational experience, including facing the military draft, gave young Americans an unusual sense of collective identity, and many of them began questioning the consumerism, conformity, and traditional social expectations that had defined the previous decade.

The movement took shape around a rejection of mainstream norms rather than a single organization or leader. Participants, often called hippies, experimented with communal living, Eastern religious and spiritual practices, and mind altering drugs such as marijuana and LSD, and they challenged conventional expectations around sex, gender roles, and authority more broadly. San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury neighborhood became a symbolic center of the movement, drawing thousands of young people during the Summer of Love in 1967.

Music served as both the soundtrack and a unifying force for the counterculture, with artists such as Bob Dylan, the Beatles, Jimi Hendrix, and Janis Joplin giving voice to its values of freedom and rebellion. The movement's cultural high point came at the Woodstock Music and Art Fair in August 1969 in upstate New York, where several hundred thousand people gathered for a festival that became an enduring symbol of the era, celebrated for its communal spirit despite crowded, muddy, and chaotic conditions.

The counterculture and the anti-war movement overlapped heavily in the people involved, and opposition to the Vietnam War was one of the counterculture's central political causes, but the counterculture itself was broader than any single protest movement, encompassing lifestyle, art, and personal rebellion alongside politics. Many Americans viewed the counterculture with alarm, seeing its rejection of traditional values as a threat to social order, and that backlash helped fuel a more conservative political shift in the years that followed, even as elements of countercultural style and attitude gradually filtered into mainstream American life.
